title: The Song of All Is Well, with Its Commentary

inline.s: Excerpted from Dream of the Red Chamber

In the southeast lies the city of Suzhou, and within it the Chang Gate is one of the finest haunts of wealth and elegance in the mortal world. Outside the Chang Gate runs Ten-Mile Street, and within the street there is a lane called Benevolence and Purity, and within that lane an old temple, which, being cramped and narrow, was called by everyone the Gourd Temple. Beside the temple lived a man who had retired from office to his village home — his surname was Zhen, his given name Fei, his style Shiyin. His wife, of the Feng clan, was gentle and virtuous and well versed in ritual. Though the family was not especially wealthy, it was reckoned among the leading clans of the district. Since Zhen Shiyin was of a placid and unworldly temperament that set no store by fame or office, he spent his days delighting in flowers and bamboo, in pouring wine and composing verse, and was altogether a man of immortal mould. One thing alone was wanting: though past fifty he had no son, only a daughter of three, nicknamed Yinglian.
One day, in the long daylight of high summer, Shiyin sat idly in his study

Wearied, he laid down his book and dozed over the desk, and in his dream he wandered to a place he could not make out. ... All at once a thunderclap seemed to split the mountains and level the earth. Shiyin gave a great shout, and when he fixed his eyes he saw the sun blazing and the plantain swaying in the breeze; half of his dream was already forgotten. Then the wet nurse came forward carrying Yinglian. Seeing his daughter more lovely than ever, like a doll of carved and polished jade, and full of life, he reached out and took her into his arms to play with her awhile, and then carried her out to the street to watch the bustle of the festival.
Truly, in idle hours time glides easily by, and (shū

how swiftly) all at once it was the Lantern Festival again. Shiyin bade his manservant Huo Qi carry Yinglian out to see the festive folk-plays — stilt-walkers, land-boats, hobby-horses, yangge dances, dragon lanterns, lion dances — and the flower lanterns. In the middle of the night Huo Qi, needing to relieve himself, set Yinglian down to sit on a doorway threshold. When he had done and came to take her up, there was no trace of Yinglian

Frantic, Huo Qi searched half the night. When dawn came and she was still nowhere to be found, he dared not return to face his master and fled instead to another region. Husband and wife, seeing their daughter had not come home all night, knew that something was wrong; they sent several others to seek her, and all returned saying there was no sign of her at all. They had borne but this one daughter in half a lifetime, and now in a moment she was lost — what anguish was theirs! So they wept day and night, almost heedless of their own lives.

Nearly a month passed, and Shiyin had fallen ill; his wife, Madam Feng, too sickened from longing for her daughter, until they sought the doctor and the diviner every day. Then, on the fifteenth of the third month, while offerings were being fried in the Gourd Temple, the monk, careless, let the oil flame leap out and set the window paper alight. The households hereabouts were all of bamboo fences and wooden walls, and it was their destined doom; so the fire spread from one to another, pulling that whole street into a blaze like Flaming Mountain. Though officers and common folk alike came to fight it, the fire had already gotten the upper hand — how could it be put down

It burned the whole night before it died, and no one could tell how many homes were consumed. Only pity poor Zhen — his house stood next door and was soon a heap of rubble; only the lives of husband, wife, and a few servants were spared. In his distress Shiyin could do naught but stamp his foot and sigh. He consulted his wife, and they resolved to move to a farm. But in those years drought and flood had ruined the harvests, bandits rose in swarms, and with officers sent to hunt them down the farmlands were unsafe besides; so he was forced to sell off his fields and betake himself, with his wife and two maids, to his father-in-law's house.

His father-in-law was named Feng Su, a native of Daruzhou. Though he was a farmer, the family was in easy circumstances. Seeing his son-in-law arrive in such reduced and sorry state, he was somewhat displeased. Fortunately Shiyin still had the silver from the sale of his property, and he took it out, entrusting Feng Su to buy some land and houses with it to provide for their future days. Feng Su, however, made use of the half and pocketed the profits, giving Shiyin only some thin fields and a broken-down house. Shiyin was a scholar, unused to farming and household management, and after struggling on for a year or two he grew poorer still. Whenever they met Feng Su would make cutting remarks; and both to his face and behind his back he complained that his son-in-law could not manage, that he was good for nothing but eating his fill and idling. Shiyin, knowing he had thrown himself upon the wrong person, could not but feel remorse; and to that was added the fright of the year before, with grief and resentment — a man in his late years, unable to withstand the joint onslaught of poverty and illness, he gradually began to show the very look of one drawing near his end.

As luck would have it, one day he hobbled out with his staff to ease his heart, and all at once he saw coming from the other direction a lame Taoist, wild and down-and-out, in straw sandals and tattered clothes, muttering these words:
Worldlings all know that the immortals are best, Yet thoughts of fame and rank will never rest;
Where are the ministers and lords of old? Their bones lie lost in grass and rime.
Worldlings all know that the immortals are best, Yet unto gold and silver ne'er they rest
From dawn till dusk they grieve their store is small, But when at last it's full, death comes to all.
Worldlings all know that the immortals are best, Yet their fond arms for a fair wife ne'er rest
She swears while you live that her love is true; When you are gone, she follows another anew.
Worldlings all know that the immortals are best, Yet their care for sons and grandsons ne'er rest
Doting parents there have been many, From of old; but filial children, where are any?

Shiyin, hearing this, went up to him and said: "You reel off a string of nonsense — all I can catch is 'All is well, all is well.'" The Taoist laughed: "If you have truly caught the words 'all is well,' then you are some way to understanding. Know that of all things in this world, good IS done with, and done with IS good. If you cannot be done with, you cannot be good; and to be good you must first be done with. This song of mine I have named 'The Song of All Is Well.'" Shiyin, who was born with a seed of past wisdom, was in his heart already fully awakened at these words, and said with a smile: "Hold on! Let me set down an annotation to your 'Song of All Is Well' — what say you?" The Taoist laughed. "Please, go ahead." So Shiyin spoke:
A mean room, an empty hall, where once the tablets of the great filled the couch.
[Tablet (
hù

) filling the couch]It pictures the height of former wealth and splendor. The allusion comes from the Old Book of Tang: when the famed Tang general Guo Ziyi, Prince of Fenyang, celebrated his sixtieth birthday, his seven sons and eight sons-in-law all came to offer congratulations. Since they were all ministers at court, each held a tablet of office; and when they came to bow, the tablets covered the ivory couch (an ivory-decorated couch) till it was full.
Withered grass and withered poplars — here once stood a place of song and dance.
Spiders' webs now fill the carved beams
(a great and wealthy house in ruin)
; green gauze now hangs on the paper window
once more
(a poor household rising in the world)
(Prosperity and decay alternate; all things change and pass.)
[Paper window]A window of grass-matting, meaning a broken and dilapidated window
What of your rouge still rich, your powder still fragrant? How is it your temples have turned to frost?
(A maiden in her bloom, in an instant an old woman with hair of white.)
Yesterday white bones were buried beneath the loess ridge; tonight, beneath the red lantern and within the curtains, a pair of mandarin ducks lie.
(While he was alive she spoke of love day after day; once he died she went off with another man.)
Chests full of gold, chests full of silver — in a turn of the hand you are a beggar all the world reviles
(in an instant become a beggar, spurned, reviled, and cursed by all)
Even as you lament that others' lives are short, little you know your own turn to come home in mourning
Well trained
(scheming by every means to rear his son into a worthy man)
, nothing guarantees he will not hereafter become a ruffian
a robber
Choosing only the fat of the land
(scheming by every means to pick out a son of a rich and noble house for his daughter to marry)
, who would have expected her to fall and be lost in the lane of flowers and smoke
(a brothel)
Because he felt the black gauze cap too small, he ended with the heavy cangue about his neck.
Yesterday he pitied his tattered padded coat for its cold; today he finds the purple-python robe
(the purple robe embroidered with the python, the ceremonial dress of high officials)
too long.
In a noisy hubbub
you have barely finished your song and I take the stage — thinking a foreign land your own home.
How utterly absurd — in the end it is all sewing a wedding gown for another's wearing
(of all the myriad things none can be carried away; only karma attends you)

[Sewing a wedding gown for another]To toil in vain for naught, and for another's benefit. From the Tang poem "The Poor Girl": "How I grieve that year after year I press the golden thread, sewing a wedding gown for another."
The mad lame Taoist, hearing this, clapped his hands and roared with laughter: "You have hit the mark

You have hit the mark!" Shiyin then said a word — "I'll be off" — snatched the shoulder-bag from the Taoist's shoulder and bore it on his own back. Without returning home, he drifted away together with the mad Taoist.
